conceptTag: What higher rates mean for a small business
readerTitle: When the bank raises rates, who pays?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주택 리모델링 업체, 철물·자재 도매상) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 금리 인상은 내 대출 이자만이 아니라 고객의 구매 결정과 재고·외상처럼 돈이 묶여 있는 모든 곳에 비용으로 들어온다.
misconception: 금리가 오르면 내 대출 이자만 조금 늘어날 뿐이다. 매출이 줄면 가격을 내려 수요를 되찾으면 된다.

sources.text: 거시경제 표준 개념 (금리의 전달 경로, 중앙은행의 긴축 정책)

factChecks.note: 금리 인상의 효과가 경제 전반에 나타나기까지 수개월 이상 걸린다는 일반적 설명만 썼습니다. 구체적 기간은 쓰지 않았습니다.
고정금리·변동금리 선택은 일반 원리로만 다루고 특정 국가의 금융·투자 조언은 하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: When the bank raises rates, who pays?
body: Maya runs a small kitchen remodeling business. Her crew is good, her reviews are great, and her prices haven't changed.
Then, in one week, three customers call to postpone their projects. None of them complain about her work. They all mention the same thing: their loan just got more expensive.

image.label: A contractor on the phone beside an unfinished kitchen
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 반쯤 완성된 주방에서 작업복 차림의 여성 사업가가 전화를 받으며 난감한 표정. 벽 달력에 'Postponed'라고 적힌 메모 세 장. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Bookings are down. What's Maya's first move?
body: Maya also has a $150,000 credit line with a variable rate, meaning the rate moves when market rates move. It just went from 5% to 9%.

options.text: Cut prices 15% to win back the postponed jobs
options.feedback: Her price didn't change; her customers' **cost of borrowing** did. A discount shrinks her margin just as her own interest bill rises, and it may not close the gap for buyers.

options.text: Map every place rates touch her business, then offer smaller, phased projects
options.feedback: This treats **interest rates** as the price of money that reaches her debt, her customers and her cash flow. Phased jobs let customers borrow less at a time.

options.text: Wait. Rates always come back down
options.feedback: Rates do move in cycles, but nobody knows the timing. Meanwhile her credit line costs $6,000 more a year.

cards.title: Higher rates reach a business three ways.
body: Most owners only watch the first line. The other two are often bigger.

breakdown.label: Your customers' debt
breakdown.detail: Yearly interest on a $40,000 remodel loan rises from $2,000 to $3,600

breakdown.label: Money that waits
breakdown.detail: Unpaid invoices and stock on shelves cost more to carry

cards.softwareNote: In software, the second channel shows up as customers cutting budgets and taking longer to sign. Investors also value distant future profits less, so raising money gets harder.

cards.title: The slowdown is the point.
body: Central banks usually raise rates to fight inflation. Higher rates make borrowing costlier, so people and businesses spend less, and price rises cool down.
So when Maya's customers delay big projects, the policy is working as intended. It isn't a strange side effect.

Two lessons follow. **First, the slowdown is real**, not a blip. Second, it arrives with a delay. Effects often build over many months, so the quiet period may last longer than the first rate rise suggests.

cards.title: Borrowed-money purchases slow first.
body: Rates hit hardest where customers pay with loans: homes, remodels, cars, machinery, furniture, business equipment.
Everyday purchases like haircuts, groceries and repairs that can't wait slow down less.

So the useful question isn't "Are rates up?" It's **"How many of my customers borrow to buy from me?"** A plumber fixing leaks and a contractor building extensions can face the same rate rise and very different years.

cards.title: Now it's a hardware wholesaler.
body: Leo supplies building materials to local contractors. He keeps $300,000 of stock, funded by a credit line now at 9%. That's $27,000 a year just to hold it, up from $15,000.
Contractors are buying less. What should he do?

options.text: Stock up now, before suppliers raise prices
options.feedback: That bet may pay off if prices jump, but every extra dollar of stock now carries a 9% **interest cost** while demand is falling.

options.text: Trim slow-moving items, keep fast sellers deep, ask suppliers for faster delivery
options.feedback: Cutting $100,000 of slow stock saves about $9,000 a year. He keeps what contractors need daily, so he doesn't lose them.

options.text: Stop all new orders until rates fall
options.feedback: It saves interest fast, but empty shelves send contractors to rivals. When the **cycle turns**, they may not come back.

cards.softwareNote: The same logic applies to a software company's cash: long annual deals paid late or heavy upfront spending cost more when money itself is pricier.

cards.title: Don't overreact to one rate move.
body: Higher rates have an upside: cash in the bank earns more, and weaker rivals may pull back.
Locking in a fixed rate buys certainty, but usually at a higher price. If rates fall, you're stuck paying more.

And rates move in cycles that nobody times well. Plan for a range of rates, not a single guess. Cut the costs that rates expose, but keep the parts of the business customers will need when demand returns.

cards.title: Find every place your business borrows or waits.
body: You used two ideas here. **Interest rates** are the price of money, and that price reaches your debt, your customers' loans and your stock. **Central bank responses** explain why: the slowdown is intended, and it arrives with a delay.
**Try it today:** list your debt, how many customers borrow to buy from you, and how much cash sits in stock or unpaid invoices.
